ID.citation: Idaho Big Game 2026 Seasons and Rules, p. 95
ID.detail: Exact point times are calculated for every CERTIFIED unit, from the half-hour-before-sunrise to half-hour-after-sunset rule. The timezone was established per UNIT rather than per state: 49 CFR § 71.9(a) runs the mountain/Pacific line along the Idaho County / Lemhi County boundary and then the main channel of the Salmon River, so no point can be placed on a side of the river — but Idaho County's own polygon (Census TIGERweb) used as a spatial filter against IDFG's GMU service shows 22 units intersecting it and NONE of the 42 certified units among them. Counties tile, so no certified unit is north of it either. A unit NOT in the certified set still gets no clock, which is why this is scoped rather than statewide.
ID.unitsWithoutAClock: The 22 units intersecting Idaho County — 10, 10A, 11, 11A, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 16A, 17, 18, 19, 19A, 20, 20A, 21, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27 — cannot be zoned from a county at all, because the river cuts the county. Their remedy is the Salmon River channel, not another county read.

MT.citation: 2026 Montana Upland Game Bird Hunting Regulations, p. 4

WA.detail: WASHINGTON IS NOT A SOLAR-FORMULA STATE, and it reads like one. WAC 220-416-020(1) says "The following tables show the lawful hunting hours (1/2 hour before sunrise to 1/2 hour after sunset)" — the parenthetical states how the tables were BUILT; the tables are the rule. There are SEVEN of them, subsections (3) to (9), selected by the weekday 1 September falls on; each splits into Western and Eastern Washington with its own A.M. and P.M. columns; rows are week-long date bands; the table is explicitly partitioned into a daylight-saving block and a Pacific-standard block with one transition row; times are wall-clock rounded to five minutes. The rule is certified and cited. No exact clock is offered because the rows have not been transcribed, and computing one from the parenthetical would return times that disagree with the printed ones — which are the law. The AUTHORITY_TABLE basis exists to hold them when they are read.

PA.detail: A TABLE, ADJUSTED BY LONGITUDE, RE-ENACTED EVERY LICENCE YEAR. § 141.4: "wild birds and mammals may be hunted 1/2 hour before sunrise to 1/2 hour after sunset AS ILLUSTRATED IN APPENDIX G" — and Appendix G is a fixed statewide table of begin-A.M./end-P.M. clock times per date range for the licence year, plus a SECOND table for migratory game birds, with a codified longitude adjustment whose meridian bands Pennsylvania publishes as a GIS layer. Three things follow. (1) It is not a point solar calculation, so the AUTHORITY_TABLE basis is the correct one. (2) It is temporal in the strongest sense: § 141.4 was amended 29 May 2026, effective 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, 56 Pa.B. 3128, so the rule is re-enacted annually and must be evaluated against the hunt date rather than cached. (3) Its codified exceptions are not adjustments to one window but different windows: furbearers — raccoon, fox, skunk, opossum, coyote, bobcat, weasel — may be hunted ANY HOUR, DAY OR NIGHT; spring turkey runs to 12 noon until the third Saturday and to half an hour after sunset thereafter; migratory birds close AT SUNSET except in the snow goose conservation and September resident goose seasons. Also unresolved and recorded in the map findings: the meridian-band layer itself has 7 bands on the Commission's ArcGIS Online account and 6 on its own server.

rootDefinition.statedAs: "Daylight hours" means the period from one-half (1/2) hour before sunrise to one-half (1/2) hour after sunset.

KY.detail: A DEFINED TERM, AND SEARCHING FOR THE TIMES PRODUCES A FALSE ABSENCE. Kentucky's species regulations mostly state no times at all — they prohibit taking outside "daylight hours" — and KRS 150.010(8) defines that once for the whole chapter. A first pass searching 301 KAR 2:172 for "sunrise" found nothing and nearly recorded deer as having no hours rule. The rule is there, by defined term. Positive control on the statute: it is "150.010 Definitions for chapter" with 46 defined terms. No published table exists: across the 40-page guide (153,696 characters extracted) "sunrise/sunset table", "table of sunrise" and "appendix" each return 0 hits, with a positive control on the same text finding "shooting hours" 10 times, "telecheck" 41 and "hunter orange" 33 — so the zero is a true zero. Kentucky's astronomy is therefore reproducible, unlike Washington's or Pennsylvania's. One presentation caveat: Kentucky counties are split between Eastern and Central time, and Ky_County_Polygons_WM carries no time-zone field, so the displayed clock needs that mapping from elsewhere.

FL.detail: THE OPPOSITE OF WASHINGTON: the offset-looking sentence IS the law, and there is no table for it to fail to reproduce. Rule 68A-13.001(4) makes hours per-species by construction — "No person shall take any game during the open season at any time other than during the shooting hours established for the species." Tested rather than assumed: all 44 pages of FWC's 2026-2027 brochure were extracted and ZERO pages contain eight or more clock times of the form h:mm, and the brochure instead tells hunters the Fish|Hunt FL app gives sunrise/sunset times. Florida spans Eastern and Central time (the panhandle west of the Apalachicola River); sunrise and sunset are solar so the computation is zone-independent, but any clock SHOWN must be rendered in the point's own civil zone, and neither the rule nor the brochure performs that conversion.

IL.detail: TWELVE DISTINCT ANSWERS AND THREE DIFFERENT TURKEY RULES IN ONE STATE. IDNR itself says the basis is solar rather than a table — "Use government sources, such as NOAA or National Weather Service, to find the sunrise-sunset times for your hunting date and location" — which is the strongest form this answer can take. No table exists: across the 60-page digest "TABLE"/"Table" occurs zero times and no appendix is referenced. The variants are legally different, not cosmetic: upland game is "Sunrise until sunset" with NO offset, so applying the deer rule there would create an hour of illegal hunting every day.

IA.detail: THE STATE THAT PROVES NO_RESTRICTION MUST BE ITS OWN STATE. Five Iowa species state affirmatively that there are no hours restrictions, in the codified rules AND independently in the booklet's SHOOTING HOURS column printing "No Restrictions". Encoding half-an-hour-before-sunrise for them would invent a restriction the authority does not impose, which §8 treats as seriously as inventing a permission. Iowa also has genuine FIXED CIVIL CLOCK rules (pheasant, partridge and quail at 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) and a species whose offset differs BY LICENCE TYPE. The statute was checked too: Iowa Code ch. 481A and ch. 483A contain NO statutory hunting-hours provision, with a positive control run for that absence. No zone-specific or longitude-specific time provision appears anywhere in IAC 571, so Iowa presents no Atikokan-style split — though that all of Iowa observes a single civil zone was not independently verified from a primary source, and must be before the 8 a.m. rules are rendered as local clock times.

IN.citation: Indiana April 2026 – March 2027 Hunting & Trapping Seasons
IN.detail: FOUR DISTINCT RULES AND TWENTY SPECIES THE AUTHORITY IS SILENT ABOUT. The official artifact states hours for five species and for nothing else. Applying the deer rule to turkey adds up to half an hour of illegal shooting time; applying it to doves adds a full hour. Raccoon and opossum are night-hunted in Indiana, so a silent inheritance of the deer offsets would not merely be unsupported — it would be substantively wrong. Indiana states plain solar offsets with no table, no "see appendix", no longitude adjustment and no printed times, so unlike Washington and Pennsylvania the statewide rule is genuinely computable. A PROPOSED interim rule capping scheduled hunts at 4:00 p.m. was found and is NOT encoded: its own header reads "Proposed Interim Rule / LSA Document #XX-XXX" with unfilled placeholders throughout, and a web-search snippet had presented that sentence as current Indiana law. The codified rule, 312 IAC Article 9, could not be retrieved by any route tried.

AL.detail: A THIRD KIND OF HOURS RULE, AND THE INVERSE OF WASHINGTON'S. Not a table dressed as a formula but a TERM WITH NO FORMULA AT ALL. r. 220-2-.05: "Legal hunting hours for game birds during the open season shall be daylight hours only, except as otherwise provided by law or regulation." "Daylight hours" is UNDEFINED in the rule, so North Ground's astronomy cannot reproduce it — there is no numeric rule to reproduce, and choosing an offset would be inventing the law. Kentucky states the identical phrase and DEFINES it in KRS 150.010(8), which is why the same words are certifiable in one state and not the other; carrying Kentucky's definition into Alabama would be exactly the error §8 forbids. The basis is recorded as AUTHORITY_TABLE because, as with Washington, whatever fixes the window is the authority's and not ours — the difference is that Alabama has not published one. Alabama then layers computable solar offsets and fixed civil clock times onto specific species and geographies, which are not yet read.

MO.detail: Recorded now that the schema can hold it. Missouri was the first state where the one-basis-per-state shape failed, and rather than file a wrong record no record was filed at all — which left the matrix saying hours were not certified when the rules had been read and cited. Missouri's big-game window is asymmetric while migratory birds close AT sunset; spring turkey needs a public-versus-private land discriminator before its window can be stated, and its cutoff is written in a named civil clock (CDT) rather than a solar term; and squirrels state no hours at all.
